messages.content:
Parties: we represent Aventis, Inc. (Sanofi); counterparty is Revolution Medicines, Inc. (RevMed).

Rule:
ID: IP
Title: Ownership of deliverables and Customer Data
Kind: direction
Summary: We own what we pay for and everything we put in; no assignment of our IP or data to the Vendor.
Severity: critical
Category: ip-data
Position — preferred:
Customer owns deliverables and work product created for it (Vendor assigns); Vendor retains pre-existing IP and grants Customer a perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free licence to any Vendor IP embedded in deliverables; Customer retains all rights in Customer Data; no joint ownership.

Position — fallback:
Vendor owns generic tools and know-how; Customer receives a perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free licence to use, modify and sublicense deliverables for its business.

Position — walk-away:
Assignment of Customer IP or Customer Data to Vendor; joint ownership without an unrestricted right to exploit.
Detection guidance:
Ownership/assignment language: who owns "Deliverables", "Work Product", "Customer Data", improvements, feedback. Flag when Customer assigns IP or data to Vendor, when Vendor owns deliverables with no licence back, or when joint ownership is created. Vendor keeping ownership of its platform is fine.

Redline guidance:
Reverse the direction of the assignment or add the licence-back; add a Customer Data ownership sentence; delete joint ownership.

The Party leading such regulatory interactions shall, as applicable, seek permission from the Regulatory Authority for representatives of the other Party to attend any such meeting or teleconference, and such other Party shall have the right, but not the obligation, to have its representatives attend (but, unless otherwise requested by the Party responsible for such meeting, not participate in) such meetings."},{"id":"p0349","text":"6.5 Adverse Events Reporting. Following the Effective Date, but in any case prior to the Initiation of the first Clinical Trial for a Product or earlier upon the written request of either Party, the Parties shall enter into a pharmacovigilance agreement setting forth the worldwide pharmacovigilance procedures for the Parties with respect to the Products, such as safety data sharing, adverse events reporting and safety profile monitoring (the \"Pharmacovigilance Agreement\"). Such procedures shall be in accordance with, and enable the Parties to fulfill, local and national regulatory reporting obligations under Applicable Law. Each Party shall be responsible for reporting quality complaints, adverse events and safety data related to the Products 39"},{"id":"p0350","text":"to the applicable Regulatory Authorities in its territory, as well as responding to safety issues and to all requests of Regulatory Authorities related to the Products in its territory, in each case at its own cost. The initial global safety database shall be established by RevMed using its Permitted Contractors or Researchers, and RevMed shall, at RevMed's sole cost and expense, transfer such global safety database to Sanofi upon Sanofi's written request reasonably in advance of the desired transfer date, which transfer date shall be no later than [***] prior to the initiation of Sanofi's first Clinical Trial for a Product and in the form requested by Sanofi. Prior to such transfer RevMed shall provide to Sanofi all safety information obtained by RevMed for the Products prior to Sanofi's assumption of the global safety database. Each Party agrees to comply with its respective obligations under the Pharmacovigilance Agreement and to cause its Affiliates, and Sublicensees to comply with such obligations."},{"id":"p0351","text":"6.6 Notification of Threatened Action. input.quote: (b) Subject to the other terms and conditions of this Agreement (including the licenses and other rights granted under this Agreement or any Ancillary Agreement), each Party shall have the right to exploit, including license, the Joint Program Technology, without a duty of accounting or any obligation to seek consent from the other Party to exploit such Joint Program Technology. To the extent necessary to effect the foregoing in a country other than the United States, each Party grants to the other Party a nonexclusive, irrevocable, perpetual, fully-paid, worldwide license, with the right to grant sublicenses, under the granting Party's interest in Joint Program Technology, for any and all purposes
input.rationale: The IP architecture protects Sanofi and creates no prohibited transfer to RevMed. Section 10.1(a) requires each Party to obtain assignment of Program Inventions from its own Third Parties to that Party (and Section 3.4 requires subcontractor assignment, or failing that an irrevocable, perpetual, fully-paid, exclusive, royalty-free worldwide licence with sublicensing rights to the engaging Party), so work generated for Sanofi vests in Sanofi; "Sanofi Sole Program Know-How"/"Sanofi Sole Program Patents" (1.109-1.110) confirm Sanofi solely owns its own Program Inventions and Section 10.4(c) gives Sanofi sole enforcement of them. Joint Program Technology is jointly owned but each Party may exploit and license it with no duty of accounting and no consent, backed by a perpetual, irrevocable, fully-paid, worldwide, sublicensable cross-licence — i.e. joint ownership with an unrestricted right to exploit, which sits at the fallback rather than the "no joint ownership" preferred position and is therefore acceptable. Sanofi's data and regulatory position are preserved and enhanced: RevMed assigns all Regulatory Approvals (INDs/NDAs) to Sanofi (6.2), transfers the global safety database at its own cost (6.5), and Sanofi owns all Product Marks and domain names (10.5). There is no assignment of Sanofi background IP or Sanofi Sole Program Technology to RevMed: Section 3.2 is only a narrow non-exclusive, royalty-free sublicence back of RevMed's own licensed technology solely to let RevMed perform its obligations, and Section 3.6 negates implied licences. The Article XII reversion is a bargained-for, licence-based (not assignment-of-background-IP) unwind limited to Termination Products, is triggered largely by Sanofi's own convenience/change-of-control election or Sanofi default, and carries post-termination royalties payable to Sanofi (12.3(c)(ii)C). Noted but not flagged: the ownership allocation in 10.1(a) is redacted [***], so the sole/joint split is inferred from the defined terms; if the unredacted text allocated Sanofi-generated inventions to RevMed we would revisit.

You are a precise customer-side contract drafter handling one playbook rule.
Use the document tools to inspect only the clauses needed, including definitions and cross-references.
Reason about direction: identify who is bound and do not flag obligations that benefit our party.
Every quote and replace.oldText must be a verbatim substring from a tool response. Quotes must be 600 characters or fewer.
Apply the playbook's classification semantics: a clause that meets the preferred or the fallback position on its material terms is compliant — do not redline it. When a clause genuinely fails the fallback, make the smallest edit that reaches the preferred position; use fallback language only when the rule guidance or the existing bargain makes preferred disproportionate.
Comments must begin with the supplied playbook prefix, use concise first-person-plural language, and explain the change and reason.
For deviation or missing findings, call propose_redline and obtain ok:true before submit_finding.
For compliant findings, do not propose a redline. Call submit_finding exactly once, then stop calling tools.

We represent the customer.
Our party aliases: Customer, Client, Licensee, Company, Buyer, Purchaser, Subscriber, User.
Counterparty aliases: Vendor, Supplier, Provider, Service Provider, Licensor, Contractor, Consultant, Seller, Host.
Comment prefix: [Playbook].
Tone: Concise, professional, first person plural ("we"). Explain what changed and why in one or two sentences, cite the playbook position, offer the fallback where sensible, never lecture.


How to classify a clause against a rule (this is how the reviewing team reads its own playbook):
- compliant: the clause meets the preferred position, OR it meets the fallback position on its material terms. A clause at the fallback is acceptable and is not redlined; say in the rationale that it sits at the fallback.
- deviation: the clause fails the fallback on a material term, or falls into walk-away territory. Only then propose a redline.
- missing: the rule expects a clause and no usable clause exists anywhere in the document.
- Minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording (a missing reminder mechanic, a missing price-uplift cap, 'paid' versus 'paid or payable', an accepted-but-not-preferred governing law) are noted in the rationale, not flagged as deviations.
- Do not flag a clause that benefits our party. Do not flag the same commercial term twice under two rules unless both rules are independently breached.

Parties: we represent Aventis, Inc. (Sanofi); counterparty is Revolution Medicines, Inc. (RevMed).

Rule:
ID: WARRANTY
Title: Performance warranty and duration
Kind: parametric
Summary: The Vendor must stand behind its work for a meaningful period with a real remedy.
Severity: medium
Category: warranty
Position — preferred:
Services performed in a professional and workmanlike manner; deliverables/software conform to documentation for 12 months (software) or 90 days (services) with repair, replace or refund; compliance with laws; no malicious code.

Position — fallback:
90 days for software, 30 days for services; same remedies.
Position — walk-away:
"AS IS" with all warranties disclaimed and no conformance warranty at all.
Detection guidance:
Find warranty and disclaimer sections; extract the warranty period and remedy; note whether the disclaimer swallows the express warranty. A missing express warranty is a deviation (insert).

Redline guidance:
Extend the period, add the remedy sentence, carve the express warranty out of the disclaimer.
Model language:
Vendor warrants that (a) the Services will be performed in a professional and workmanlike manner consistent with industry standards; and (b) for a period of ninety (90) days following delivery, each Deliverable will conform in all material respects to its documentation. Customer's remedy for breach of this warranty is, at Vendor's option, re-performance, repair or replacement, or a refund of the fees paid for the non-conforming Services or Deliverable.

reasons: Claimed status is 'compliant' and the rendered redline is identical to the original with no comment, which is the expected output for a compliant finding.

The cited Section 15.2(a) gives our party (Sanofi, the customer/licensee) exactly the preferred carve-outs: assignment to any Affiliate without RevMed consent and assignment in whole, without consent, to a successor/purchaser in a sale of all or substantially all relevant assets or a merger/acquisition. The deterministic check confirms the successor/affiliate carve-out is present.

Vendor-side restrictions are present and directionally favourable to us: RevMed needs our consent (not unreasonably withheld, delayed or conditioned) for affiliate assignments and may not transfer the RevMed Licensed Patents to a Third Party without our consent (15.2(b)).

No RevMed right is triggered by a Change of Control of our party — the cited change-of-control mechanics (p0489) run only on RevMed's Change of Control and confer the option (terminate or elect the alternative) on us, so the walk-away trigger (vendor termination/re-pricing on Customer CoC) is absent.

RevMed's ability to assign in whole on its own Change of Control without our consent, and the absence of an express 'never to a competitor' bar, fall short of preferred but sit at or above the mutual-successor-assignment fallback and are correctly noted in the rationale rather than redlined, consistent with the playbook's classification semantics.

The residual points flagged in the rationale (post-termination royalty ending on our Change of Control under 12.3(c); withholding gross-up allocation in 9.7(a)) are financial-terms sub-elements rather than assignment restrictions, and are appropriately noted, not raised as a deviation under ASSIGN.

No RevMed right is triggered by a Change of Control of our party — the cited change-of-control mechanics (p0489) run only on RevMed's Change of Control and confer the option (terminate or elect the alternative) on us, so the walk-away trigger (vendor termination/re-pricing on Customer CoC) is absent. The residual points flagged in the rationale (post-termination royalty ending on our Change of Control under 12.3(c); withholding gross-up allocation in 9.7(a)) are financial-terms sub-elements rather than assignment restrictions, and are appropriately noted, not raised as a deviation under ASSIGN.

Parties: we represent Aventis, Inc. (Sanofi); counterparty is Revolution Medicines, Inc. (RevMed).

Rule:
ID: TRANSITION
Title: Post-termination transition assistance and data return
Kind: missing
Summary: When it ends, we get our data back and help moving.
Severity: medium
Category: transition
Position — preferred:
On expiry or termination, Vendor provides transition assistance for up to 6 months at then-current rates, returns Customer Data in a standard machine-readable format within 30 days, and certifies deletion thereafter.

Position — fallback:
90 days of transition assistance; data export within 30 days.
Position — walk-away:
No data return, or immediate deletion of Customer Data on termination.
Detection guidance:
Look for transition, exit, data return/export, deletion timing. Absence in a services/hosting agreement is a deviation (insert).
Redline guidance:
Insert a transition-assistance and data-return paragraph in the termination section.
Model language:
Upon expiry or termination of this Agreement for any reason, Vendor shall (a) at Customer's request, provide reasonable transition assistance for up to six (6) months at Vendor's then-current rates; (b) within thirty (30) days, return all Customer Data in a commonly used, machine-readable format; and (c) thereafter delete Customer Data from its systems and certify such deletion in writing.

input.rationale: The Agreement contains no liquidated damages, penalty or minimum-fee provision payable by Sanofi (our party). Searches for "liquidated damages" and "penalty" return nothing; the financial provisions (Article IX) impose only upfront, milestone, royalty and profit/loss-share payments tied to actual performance, and the sole late-payment consequence is ordinary reciprocal interest at LIBOR + [***]% capped at the maximum lawful rate (Section 9.6), which the rule expressly treats as not a liquidated-damages deviation. Termination by Sanofi for convenience under Section 12.2(a)(i) requires only notice, with no early-termination or minimum fee; the post-termination royalty flow in Section 12.3(c)(ii)C runs from RevMed to Sanofi and so benefits us. For diligence failures under Section 5.7, Section 12.6 makes termination the exception to the "not sole remedy" rule rather than imposing a fixed sum. This meets the preferred position (no liquidated damages or penalties payable by Customer), so no redline is warranted.

**Finding: compliant (no redline).**

The IP package works for Sanofi:

- **Ownership of what we generate:** §10.1(a) requires each Party's Third Parties to assign Program Inventions to *that* Party, and §3.4 backstops this with an assignment-or-perpetual-exclusive-licence covenant for subcontractors. Definitions 1.109–1.110 ("Sanofi Sole Program Know-How"/"Patents") confirm Sanofi solely owns its own Program Inventions, with sole enforcement under §10.4(c).
- **Joint ownership:** present, but with an *unrestricted* right to exploit and license, no duty of accounting, no consent, plus a perpetual, irrevocable, fully-paid, worldwide, sublicensable cross-licence. That sits at the **fallback**, not walk-away territory (which is joint ownership *without* free exploitation), so it is acceptable and not redlined.
- **Our data/regulatory assets:** RevMed assigns all Regulatory Approvals (INDs/NDAs) to Sanofi (§6.2) and transfers the global safety database at its own cost (§6.5); Sanofi owns all Product Marks and domain names (§10.5).
- **No transfer of our IP to RevMed:** §3.2 is a narrow non-exclusive, royalty-free sublicence back of *RevMed's own* technology solely to perform its obligations; §3.6 negates implied licences. The Article XII reversion is licence-based, limited to Termination Products, largely triggered by Sanofi's own election or default, and royalty-bearing in Sanofi's favour.

One item flagged in the rationale rather than redlined: the allocation text in **§10.1(a) is redacted [***]**, so the sole/joint split is inferred from the defined terms — worth confirming against the unredacted text before signature.

You are an independent verifier of one proposed contract finding.
Judge the proposal against the supplied playbook rule, original paragraphs, resolved definitions, deterministic checks, rendered redline, and comment.
Do not rely on hidden drafter reasoning. Fail invalid, directionally wrong, or rule-incomplete edits.
Deterministic checks are heuristics (regular expressions and a changed-character ratio), not verdicts: a failed regex may simply be a phrasing variant, and a high changed-character ratio is acceptable when the rule genuinely requires rewriting the clause (for example replacing a governing-law sentence or deleting a take-or-pay obligation). Weigh them as evidence and decide on substance: does the redline reach the playbook position with the smallest edit that does so, and is the comment accurate?
The claimed status matters: for a compliant finding, no redline or counterparty comment is expected, and you should pass when the cited text supports compliance. Fail a deviation finding whose cited clause already meets the preferred or the fallback position on its material terms (the playbook's classification semantics) — a redline that merely upgrades an acceptable fallback to preferred wording is over-flagging. Compliant findings are retained as internal evaluation evidence, not raised as negotiation issues. For deviation or missing findings, require an actionable valid proposal.
Return a concise verdict with actionable reasons.

We represent the customer.
Our party aliases: Customer, Client, Licensee, Company, Buyer, Purchaser, Subscriber, User.
Counterparty aliases: Vendor, Supplier, Provider, Service Provider, Licensor, Contractor, Consultant, Seller, Host.
Comment prefix: [Playbook].
Tone: Concise, professional, first person plural ("we"). Explain what changed and why in one or two sentences, cite the playbook position, offer the fallback where sensible, never lecture.


How to classify a clause against a rule (this is how the reviewing team reads its own playbook):
- compliant: the clause meets the preferred position, OR it meets the fallback position on its material terms. A clause at the fallback is acceptable and is not redlined; say in the rationale that it sits at the fallback.
- deviation: the clause fails the fallback on a material term, or falls into walk-away territory. Only then propose a redline.
- missing: the rule expects a clause and no usable clause exists anywhere in the document.
- Minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording (a missing reminder mechanic, a missing price-uplift cap, 'paid' versus 'paid or payable', an accepted-but-not-preferred governing law) are noted in the rationale, not flagged as deviations.
- Do not flag a clause that benefits our party. Do not flag the same commercial term twice under two rules unless both rules are independently breached.

Rule:
ID: IP
Title: Ownership of deliverables and Customer Data
Kind: direction
Summary: We own what we pay for and everything we put in; no assignment of our IP or data to the Vendor.
Severity: critical
Category: ip-data
Position — preferred:
Customer owns deliverables and work product created for it (Vendor assigns); Vendor retains pre-existing IP and grants Customer a perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free licence to any Vendor IP embedded in deliverables; Customer retains all rights in Customer Data; no joint ownership.

Position — fallback:
Vendor owns generic tools and know-how; Customer receives a perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free licence to use, modify and sublicense deliverables for its business.

Position — walk-away:
Assignment of Customer IP or Customer Data to Vendor; joint ownership without an unrestricted right to exploit.
Detection guidance:
Ownership/assignment language: who owns "Deliverables", "Work Product", "Customer Data", improvements, feedback. Flag when Customer assigns IP or data to Vendor, when Vendor owns deliverables with no licence back, or when joint ownership is created. Vendor keeping ownership of its platform is fine.

Redline guidance:
Reverse the direction of the assignment or add the licence-back; add a Customer Data ownership sentence; delete joint ownership.

Claimed finding status: compliant

Finding rationale:
The IP architecture protects Sanofi and creates no prohibited transfer to RevMed. Section 10.1(a) requires each Party to obtain assignment of Program Inventions from its own Third Parties to that Party (and Section 3.4 requires subcontractor assignment, or failing that an irrevocable, perpetual, fully-paid, exclusive, royalty-free worldwide licence with sublicensing rights to the engaging Party), so work generated for Sanofi vests in Sanofi; "Sanofi Sole Program Know-How"/"Sanofi Sole Program Patents" (1.109-1.110) confirm Sanofi solely owns its own Program Inventions and Section 10.4(c) gives Sanofi sole enforcement of them. Joint Program Technology is jointly owned but each Party may exploit and license it with no duty of accounting and no consent, backed by a perpetual, irrevocable, fully-paid, worldwide, sublicensable cross-licence — i.e. joint ownership with an unrestricted right to exploit, which sits at the fallback rather than the "no joint ownership" preferred position and is therefore acceptable. Sanofi's data and regulatory position are preserved and enhanced: RevMed assigns all Regulatory Approvals (INDs/NDAs) to Sanofi (6.2), transfers the global safety database at its own cost (6.5), and Sanofi owns all Product Marks and domain names (10.5). There is no assignment of Sanofi background IP or Sanofi Sole Program Technology to RevMed: Section 3.2 is only a narrow non-exclusive, royalty-free sublicence back of RevMed's own licensed technology solely to let RevMed perform its obligations, and Section 3.6 negates implied licences. The Article XII reversion is a bargained-for, licence-based unwind limited to Termination Products, triggered largely by Sanofi's own convenience/change-of-control election or Sanofi default, and carries post-termination royalties payable to Sanofi (12.3(c)(ii)C). Noted but not flagged: the ownership allocation in 10.1(a) is redacted [***], so the sole/joint split is inferred from the defined terms; if the unredacted text allocated Sanofi-generated inventions to RevMed we would revisit.

input.quote: 14.6 Insurance. Each Party shall procure and maintain insurance, including product liability insurance, with respect to its activities hereunder and under the Ancillary Agreements and which is consistent with normal business practices of companies similarly situated at all times during which any SHP2 Inhibitors or Product is being clinically tested in human subjects or commercially distributed or sold. Sanofi may fulfill such obligation through self- insurance. Each Party shall provide the other Party with evidence of such insurance upon request
input.rationale: An insurance clause is present (Section 14.6), so the rule's "missing" trigger is not met. RevMed is bound to procure and maintain insurance — expressly including product liability cover, the line most relevant to a clinical/commercial collaboration of this kind — at levels consistent with normal business practices of similarly situated companies, for the whole period during which SHP2 Inhibitors or Product are in human clinical testing or commercial distribution. The clause also delivers the two mechanics the playbook cares about beyond limits: evidence of insurance on request, and (one-way in our favour) advance written notice from RevMed of cancellation, non-renewal or material change. It further confirms that insurance does not cap either Party's Article XIV indemnification obligations, preserving our recovery against RevMed. Several terms run in our favour and should not be flagged: the obligation is mutual, and Sanofi alone may satisfy it through self-insurance. On its material terms this sits at the fallback rather than the preferred position. Noted but not flagged: there are no stated dollar limits (no CGL 1M/2M, no E&O, no cyber/privacy tower) and no one-year tail after the term. Those preferred-position specifics are of limited weight here because RevMed is a licensor/co-development counterparty rather than a hosting or data-processing vendor — it does not host our systems or work on our premises, so the walk-away scenario (no insurance for a vendor processing personal data or working on-site) is not engaged. Per the playbook's classification semantics, these are sub-elements short of preferred wording and are recorded in the rationale rather than redlined.

input.quote: 14.6 Insurance. Each Party shall procure and maintain insurance, including product liability insurance, with respect to its activities hereunder and under the Ancillary Agreements and which is consistent with normal business practices of companies similarly situated at all times during which any SHP2 Inhibitors or Product is being clinically tested in human subjects or commercially distributed or sold. Sanofi may fulfill such obligation through self- insurance. Each Party shall provide the other Party with evidence of such insurance upon request
input.rationale: An insurance clause is present (Section 14.6), so the rule's "missing" trigger is not met. RevMed is bound to procure and maintain insurance — expressly including product liability cover, the line most relevant to a clinical/commercial collaboration of this kind — at levels consistent with normal business practices of similarly situated companies, for the whole period during which SHP2 Inhibitors or Product are in human clinical testing or commercial distribution. The clause also delivers the two mechanics the playbook cares about beyond limits: evidence of insurance on request, and (one-way in our favour) advance written notice from RevMed of cancellation, non-renewal or material change. It further confirms that insurance does not cap either Party's Article XIV indemnification obligations, preserving our recovery against RevMed. Several terms run in our favour and should not be flagged: the obligation is mutual, and Sanofi alone may satisfy it through self-insurance. On its material terms this sits at the fallback rather than the preferred position. Noted but not flagged: there are no stated dollar limits (no CGL 1M/2M, no E&O, no cyber/privacy tower) and no one-year tail after the term. Those preferred-position specifics are of limited weight here because RevMed is a licensor/co-development counterparty rather than a hosting or data-processing vendor — it does not host our systems or work on our premises, so the walk-away scenario (no insurance for a vendor processing personal data or working on-site) is not engaged. Per the playbook's classification semantics, these are sub-elements short of preferred wording and are recorded in the rationale rather than redlined.

input.quote: 13.5 No Other Warranties. EXCEPT AS EXPRESSLY STATED IN THIS ARTICLE XIII, (A) NO REPRESENTATION, CONDITION OR WARRANTY WHATSOEVER IS MADE OR GIVEN BY OR ON BEHALF OF SANOFI OR REVMED; AND (B) ALL OTHER CONDITIONS AND WARRANTIES WHETHER WRITTEN OR ORAL OR EXPRESS OR IMPLIED ARE HEREBY EXPRESSLY EXCLUDED, INCLUDING ANY CONDITIONS AND WARRANTIES OF MERCHANTABILITY, FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE OR NON-INFRINGEMENT.
input.rationale:
This is a drug research/development and commercialization collaboration, not a services or software purchase, so the rule's parameters map onto RevMed's performance standards and warranty package rather than a fixed software/deliverable conformance period. The material protections the rule targets are all present and sit at or above the fallback:

1. Performance standard (the "professional and workmanlike" analogue): Section 4.2(b) (p0291) and Section 5.2(b) (p0313) require RevMed to perform all Research and Development activities "in compliance with all Applicable Law (including GMP, GLP and GCP)" and to use diligent efforts to conduct activities in accordance with each Research/Development Plan, including timelines. GMP/GLP/GCP is the industry-standard equivalent of the preferred workmanlike/industry-standards covenant.

2. Real remedy: Sections 4.2(b) and 5.2(b) give a graduated cure mechanic (JRDC/JSC-specified cure actions, cure periods) followed by Sanofi step-in/transfer rights "without prejudice to any other rights or remedies Sanofi may have under this Agreement or otherwise at law or in equity" (p0292, p0314). Re-performance and cure are therefore backed by full retained remedies, plus RevMed indemnifies Sanofi for material breach of its warranties (p0583) and material breach supports termination. This is a stronger remedy than the rule's repair/replace/refund floor.

3. Compliance with laws: warranted at Section 13.2(u) (p0564) and covenanted mutually at Section 13.4(b) (p0572).

4. Express warranty not swallowed by the disclaimer: Section 13.5 opens with "EXCEPT AS EXPRESSLY STATED IN THIS ARTICLE XIII," which preserves the entire Article XIII package — RevMed's twenty-one express representations and warranties in Section 13.2 (p0543 et seq.) covering sole ownership free of liens, no prior encumbrance, right to grant the licenses, non-infringement, non-misappropriation, patent validity and enforceability, no litigation, no government-funding encumbrance, and completeness of diligence disclosures. This is the opposite of the walk-away "AS IS with all warranties disclaimed" position.

5. Product conformance: Section 7.3 (p0360) defers conformance to a negotiated Supply Agreement and Quality Agreement, which "shall cover the documentation and other quality requirements for the acceptance of previously manufactured supply of Product" — the correct home for batch-level conformance and acceptance/rejection remedies in a pharma collaboration.

Sub-elements short of the preferred wording, noted rather than flagged: there is no fixed-duration (12-month/90-day) conformance-to-documentation warranty with an express repair/replace/refund election, and no "no malicious code" warranty — neither maps to this deal type, as there is no software or discrete deliverable, and product conformance is expressly routed to the Supply and Quality Agreements. Two minor points to track rather than redline here: (a) the Section 13.2 warranties are given only "as of the Execution Date," which is standard for a transaction of this type and is supplemented by the forward-looking covenants in Sections 13.3 and 13.4; and (b) when negotiating the Supply and Quality Agreements under Section 7.3 we should secure an express batch conformance warranty (GMP, specifications, no adulteration) with replacement-or-refund remedies, and confirm Section 13.5 is not read to reach warranties given in those Ancillary Agreements.

No redline proposed — the clause meets the fallback on its material terms and the disclaimer benefits from a proper carve-out, so flagging would be counterproductive.

You are a precise customer-side contract drafter handling one playbook rule.
Use the document tools to inspect only the clauses needed, including definitions and cross-references.
Reason about direction: identify who is bound and do not flag obligations that benefit our party.
Every quote and replace.oldText must be a verbatim substring from a tool response. Quotes must be 600 characters or fewer.
Apply the playbook's classification semantics: a clause that meets the preferred or the fallback position on its material terms is compliant — do not redline it. When a clause genuinely fails the fallback, make the smallest edit that reaches the preferred position; use fallback language only when the rule guidance or the existing bargain makes preferred disproportionate.
Comments must begin with the supplied playbook prefix, use concise first-person-plural language, and explain the change and reason.
For deviation or missing findings, call propose_redline and obtain ok:true before submit_finding.
For compliant findings, do not propose a redline. Call submit_finding exactly once, then stop calling tools.

We represent the customer.
Our party aliases: Customer, Client, Licensee, Company, Buyer, Purchaser, Subscriber, User.
Counterparty aliases: Vendor, Supplier, Provider, Service Provider, Licensor, Contractor, Consultant, Seller, Host.
Comment prefix: [Playbook].
Tone: Concise, professional, first person plural ("we"). Explain what changed and why in one or two sentences, cite the playbook position, offer the fallback where sensible, never lecture.


How to classify a clause against a rule (this is how the reviewing team reads its own playbook):
- compliant: the clause meets the preferred position, OR it meets the fallback position on its material terms. A clause at the fallback is acceptable and is not redlined; say in the rationale that it sits at the fallback.
- deviation: the clause fails the fallback on a material term, or falls into walk-away territory. Only then propose a redline.
- missing: the rule expects a clause and no usable clause exists anywhere in the document.
- Minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording (a missing reminder mechanic, a missing price-uplift cap, 'paid' versus 'paid or payable', an accepted-but-not-preferred governing law) are noted in the rationale, not flagged as deviations.
- Do not flag a clause that benefits our party. Do not flag the same commercial term twice under two rules unless both rules are independently breached.

messages.content:
Parties: we represent Aventis, Inc. (Sanofi); counterparty is Revolution Medicines, Inc. (RevMed).

Rule:
ID: WARRANTY
Title: Performance warranty and duration
Kind: parametric
Summary: The Vendor must stand behind its work for a meaningful period with a real remedy.
Severity: medium
Category: warranty
Position — preferred:
Services performed in a professional and workmanlike manner; deliverables/software conform to documentation for 12 months (software) or 90 days (services) with repair, replace or refund; compliance with laws; no malicious code.

Position — fallback:
90 days for software, 30 days for services; same remedies.
Position — walk-away:
"AS IS" with all warranties disclaimed and no conformance warranty at all.
Detection guidance:
Find warranty and disclaimer sections; extract the warranty period and remedy; note whether the disclaimer swallows the express warranty. A missing express warranty is a deviation (insert).

Redline guidance:
Extend the period, add the remedy sentence, carve the express warranty out of the disclaimer.
Model language:
Vendor warrants that (a) the Services will be performed in a professional and workmanlike manner consistent with industry standards; and (b) for a period of ninety (90) days following delivery, each Deliverable will conform in all material respects to its documentation. Customer's remedy for breach of this warranty is, at Vendor's option, re-performance, repair or replacement, or a refund of the fees paid for the non-conforming Services or Deliverable.

input.rationale:
This is a drug research/development and commercialization collaboration, not a services or software purchase, so the rule's parameters map onto RevMed's performance standards and warranty package rather than a fixed software/deliverable conformance period. The material protections the rule targets are all present and sit at or above the fallback:

1. Performance standard (the "professional and workmanlike" analogue): Section 4.2(b) (p0291) and Section 5.2(b) (p0313) require RevMed to perform all Research and Development activities "in compliance with all Applicable Law (including GMP, GLP and GCP)" and to use diligent efforts to conduct activities in accordance with each Research/Development Plan, including timelines. GMP/GLP/GCP is the industry-standard equivalent of the preferred workmanlike/industry-standards covenant.

2. Real remedy: Sections 4.2(b) and 5.2(b) give a graduated cure mechanic (JRDC/JSC-specified cure actions, cure periods) followed by Sanofi step-in/transfer rights "without prejudice to any other rights or remedies Sanofi may have under this Agreement or otherwise at law or in equity" (p0292, p0314). Re-performance and cure are therefore backed by full retained remedies, plus RevMed indemnifies Sanofi for material breach of its warranties (p0583) and material breach supports termination. This is a stronger remedy than the rule's repair/replace/refund floor.

3. Compliance with laws: warranted at Section 13.2(u) (p0564) and covenanted mutually at Section 13.4(b) (p0572).

4. Express warranty not swallowed by the disclaimer: Section 13.5 opens with "EXCEPT AS EXPRESSLY STATED IN THIS ARTICLE XIII," which preserves the entire Article XIII package — RevMed's twenty-one express representations and warranties in Section 13.2 (p0543 et seq.) covering sole ownership free of liens, no prior encumbrance, right to grant the licenses, non-infringement, non-misappropriation, patent validity and enforceability, no litigation, no government-funding encumbrance, and completeness of diligence disclosures. This is the opposite of the walk-away "AS IS with all warranties disclaimed" position.

5. Product conformance: Section 7.3 (p0360) defers conformance to a negotiated Supply Agreement and Quality Agreement, which "shall cover the documentation and other quality requirements for the acceptance of previously manufactured supply of Product" — the correct home for batch-level conformance and acceptance/rejection remedies in a pharma collaboration.

Sub-elements short of the preferred wording, noted rather than flagged: there is no fixed-duration (12-month/90-day) conformance-to-documentation warranty with an express repair/replace/refund election, and no "no malicious code" warranty — neither maps to this deal type, as there is no software or discrete deliverable, and product conformance is expressly routed to the Supply and Quality Agreements. Two minor points to track rather than redline here: (a) the Section 13.2 warranties are given only "as of the Execution Date," which is standard for a transaction of this type and is supplemented by the forward-looking covenants in Sections 13.3 and 13.4; and (b) when negotiating the Supply and Quality Agreements under Section 7.3 we should secure an express batch conformance warranty (GMP, specifications, no adulteration) with replacement-or-refund remedies, and confirm Section 13.5 is not read to reach warranties given in those Ancillary Agreements.

No redline proposed — the clause meets the fallback on its material terms and the disclaimer benefits from a proper carve-out, so flagging would be counterproductive.

**Finding: Compliant** (rule LD — Liquidated damages and penalties payable by Customer)

I reviewed the financial provisions (Art. IX), termination and effects-of-termination provisions (Art. XII), and the liability/indemnification article (Art. XIV), plus full-text searches for "liquidated damages" and "penalty" (no hits).

Key points:
- **No Customer-payable LD or penalty exists.** Sanofi's payment obligations are limited to the $50M upfront, capped milestones ($520M aggregate), royalties on Net Sales, and the U.S. profit/loss share — all performance-linked, not penal.
- **Late-payment interest only** (§ 9.6): reciprocal, LIBOR + [***]%, capped at the maximum lawful rate. The rule's detection guidance expressly treats ordinary late-payment interest as not a deviation.
- **No early-termination fee.** § 12.2(a)(i) lets Sanofi terminate for convenience on notice alone, with no minimum fee or termination payment. The post-termination royalties in § 12.3(c)(ii)C run *from RevMed to Sanofi*, which benefits our party.
- **Diligence failure (§ 5.7)** is not backed by a fixed sum; § 12.6 carves § 5.7 out of the "termination is not the sole remedy" rule, i.e. termination is the remedy there.

This sits at the **preferred** position (no liquidated damages or penalties payable by Customer), so no redline was proposed.

system.text:
You are an independent verifier of one proposed contract finding.
Judge the proposal against the supplied playbook rule, original paragraphs, resolved definitions, deterministic checks, rendered redline, and comment.
Do not rely on hidden drafter reasoning. Fail invalid, directionally wrong, or rule-incomplete edits.
Deterministic checks are heuristics (regular expressions and a changed-character ratio), not verdicts: a failed regex may simply be a phrasing variant, and a high changed-character ratio is acceptable when the rule genuinely requires rewriting the clause (for example replacing a governing-law sentence or deleting a take-or-pay obligation). Weigh them as evidence and decide on substance: does the redline reach the playbook position with the smallest edit that does so, and is the comment accurate?
The claimed status matters: for a compliant finding, no redline or counterparty comment is expected, and you should pass when the cited text supports compliance. Fail a deviation finding whose cited clause already meets the preferred or the fallback position on its material terms (the playbook's classification semantics) — a redline that merely upgrades an acceptable fallback to preferred wording is over-flagging. Compliant findings are retained as internal evaluation evidence, not raised as negotiation issues. For deviation or missing findings, require an actionable valid proposal.
Return a concise verdict with actionable reasons.

We represent the customer.
Our party aliases: Customer, Client, Licensee, Company, Buyer, Purchaser, Subscriber, User.
Counterparty aliases: Vendor, Supplier, Provider, Service Provider, Licensor, Contractor, Consultant, Seller, Host.
Comment prefix: [Playbook].
Tone: Concise, professional, first person plural ("we"). Explain what changed and why in one or two sentences, cite the playbook position, offer the fallback where sensible, never lecture.


How to classify a clause against a rule (this is how the reviewing team reads its own playbook):
- compliant: the clause meets the preferred position, OR it meets the fallback position on its material terms. A clause at the fallback is acceptable and is not redlined; say in the rationale that it sits at the fallback.
- deviation: the clause fails the fallback on a material term, or falls into walk-away territory. Only then propose a redline.
- missing: the rule expects a clause and no usable clause exists anywhere in the document.
- Minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording (a missing reminder mechanic, a missing price-uplift cap, 'paid' versus 'paid or payable', an accepted-but-not-preferred governing law) are noted in the rationale, not flagged as deviations.
- Do not flag a clause that benefits our party. Do not flag the same commercial term twice under two rules unless both rules are independently breached.

Rule:
ID: LD
Title: Liquidated damages and penalties payable by Customer
Kind: direction
Summary: Service credits to us are welcome; liquidated damages against us are not.
Severity: high
Category: commercial
Position — preferred:
No liquidated damages or penalties payable by Customer.
Position — fallback:
Early-termination fee capped at 3 months' fees as the sole liquidated amount.
Position — walk-away:
Liquidated damages exceeding the remaining contract value or triggered by minor breaches.
Detection guidance:
Identify liquidated damages, penalties, minimum fees on termination, "shall pay … as liquidated damages". Flag only when Customer pays. Service credits or LDs payable by Vendor to Customer are compliant.

Redline guidance:
Delete the Customer-payable LD; if an early-termination fee is unavoidable, cap it at 3 months' fees.

Claimed finding status: compliant

Finding rationale:
The Agreement contains no liquidated damages, penalty or minimum-fee provision payable by Sanofi (our party). Searches for "liquidated damages" and "penalty" return nothing; the financial provisions (Article IX) impose only upfront, milestone, royalty and profit/loss-share payments tied to actual performance, and the sole late-payment consequence is ordinary reciprocal interest at LIBOR + [***]% capped at the maximum lawful rate (Section 9.6), which the rule expressly treats as not a liquidated-damages deviation. Termination by Sanofi for convenience under Section 12.2(a)(i) requires only notice, with no early-termination or minimum fee; the post-termination royalty flow in Section 12.3(c)(ii)C runs from RevMed to Sanofi and so benefits us. For diligence failures under Section 5.7, Section 12.6 makes termination the exception to the "not sole remedy" rule rather than imposing a fixed sum. This meets the preferred position (no liquidated damages or penalties payable by Customer), so no redline is warranted.

You are a precise customer-side contract drafter handling one playbook rule.
Use the document tools to inspect only the clauses needed, including definitions and cross-references.
Reason about direction: identify who is bound and do not flag obligations that benefit our party.
Every quote and replace.oldText must be a verbatim substring from a tool response. Quotes must be 600 characters or fewer.
Apply the playbook's classification semantics: a clause that meets the preferred or the fallback position on its material terms is compliant — do not redline it. When a clause genuinely fails the fallback, make the smallest edit that reaches the preferred position; use fallback language only when the rule guidance or the existing bargain makes preferred disproportionate.
Comments must begin with the supplied playbook prefix, use concise first-person-plural language, and explain the change and reason.
For deviation or missing findings, call propose_redline and obtain ok:true before submit_finding.
For compliant findings, do not propose a redline. Call submit_finding exactly once, then stop calling tools.

We represent the customer.
Our party aliases: Customer, Client, Licensee, Company, Buyer, Purchaser, Subscriber, User.
Counterparty aliases: Vendor, Supplier, Provider, Service Provider, Licensor, Contractor, Consultant, Seller, Host.
Comment prefix: [Playbook].
Tone: Concise, professional, first person plural ("we"). Explain what changed and why in one or two sentences, cite the playbook position, offer the fallback where sensible, never lecture.


How to classify a clause against a rule (this is how the reviewing team reads its own playbook):
- compliant: the clause meets the preferred position, OR it meets the fallback position on its material terms. A clause at the fallback is acceptable and is not redlined; say in the rationale that it sits at the fallback.
- deviation: the clause fails the fallback on a material term, or falls into walk-away territory. Only then propose a redline.
- missing: the rule expects a clause and no usable clause exists anywhere in the document.
- Minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording (a missing reminder mechanic, a missing price-uplift cap, 'paid' versus 'paid or payable', an accepted-but-not-preferred governing law) are noted in the rationale, not flagged as deviations.
- Do not flag a clause that benefits our party. Do not flag the same commercial term twice under two rules unless both rules are independently breached.

Parties: we represent Aventis, Inc. (Sanofi); counterparty is Revolution Medicines, Inc. (RevMed).

Rule:
ID: TRANSITION
Title: Post-termination transition assistance and data return
Kind: missing
Summary: When it ends, we get our data back and help moving.
Severity: medium
Category: transition
Position — preferred:
On expiry or termination, Vendor provides transition assistance for up to 6 months at then-current rates, returns Customer Data in a standard machine-readable format within 30 days, and certifies deletion thereafter.

Position — fallback:
90 days of transition assistance; data export within 30 days.
Position — walk-away:
No data return, or immediate deletion of Customer Data on termination.
Detection guidance:
Look for transition, exit, data return/export, deletion timing. Absence in a services/hosting agreement is a deviation (insert).
Redline guidance:
Insert a transition-assistance and data-return paragraph in the termination section.
Model language:
Upon expiry or termination of this Agreement for any reason, Vendor shall (a) at Customer's request, provide reasonable transition assistance for up to six (6) months at Vendor's then-current rates; (b) within thirty (30) days, return all Customer Data in a commonly used, machine-readable format; and (c) thereafter delete Customer Data from its systems and certify such deletion in writing.

paragraphs.text: MANUFACTURING AND SUPPLY

7.1 General. The Manufacture of the SHP2 Inhibitors and Products, including all process and formulation development in connection therewith, including Chemistry, Manufacturing and Controls (CMC) activities, shall be overseen and coordinated by (a) RevMed for clinical supply related to Phase 1 Clinical Trials, and Phase 2 Clinical Trials that are not Registrational Clinical Trials, and (b) Sanofi for supply of all Clinical Trials other than those set forth in clause (a) and all supply associated with Commercialization. If requested by the JMC, each Party shall provide reports summarizing its Manufacturing activities and the results of such activities.

7.2 Transfer of Manufacturing Know-How. Upon Sanofi's request, RevMed shall transfer to Sanofi or its designee Know-How Controlled by RevMed that is necessary or useful to enable the Manufacture of each SHP2 Inhibitor that is nominated or designated as a Development Candidate pursuant to Section 4.3, Development Candidate and Product, including regulatory starting materials and key starting materials, as set forth in this Section 7.2. Sanofi may also request such Know-How for backup SHP2 Inhibitors that Sanofi is considering for nomination or designation as a Development Candidate, and RevMed shall transfer such Know-How to Sanofi (to the extent any exists). RevMed shall (a) at [***] cost, provide copies or samples of relevant documentation (including, but not limited to, documentation listed in Exhibit K of the Correspondence), materials and other embodiments of such Know-How, (b) at [***] cost (calculated on [***]), make available RevMed's qualified technical employees, and use Commercially Reasonable Efforts to make available the qualified technical personnel of RevMed's independent manufacturing contractors, in each case, on a reasonable basis to consult with Sanofi or its designee with respect to such Know-How, and (c) if requested by Sanofi, at [***] cost, use Commercially Reasonable Efforts to support Sanofi in the establishment of its own supply agreements with Third Party suppliers of RevMed.

7.3 Supply Agreement. In each case where one Party shall Manufacture Product for the other Party for clinical use or commercial use, (with the cost and expense of the commercial supply of Product for the U.S. being subject to Section 9.4), the Parties shall negotiate in good faith to enter into a supply agreement (a "Supply Agreement") and a quality agreement (a "Quality Agreement") for such Manufacture on commercially reasonable terms. Such Supply Agreement shall cover the documentation and other quality requirements for the acceptance of previously manufactured supply of Product for use by the other Party. The price charged by the manufacturing Party under any Supply Agreement shall be equal to [***] unless otherwise agreed by the Parties. 41

You are a precise customer-side contract drafter handling one playbook rule.
Use the document tools to inspect only the clauses needed, including definitions and cross-references.
Reason about direction: identify who is bound and do not flag obligations that benefit our party.
Every quote and replace.oldText must be a verbatim substring from a tool response. Quotes must be 600 characters or fewer.
Apply the playbook's classification semantics: a clause that meets the preferred or the fallback position on its material terms is compliant — do not redline it. When a clause genuinely fails the fallback, make the smallest edit that reaches the preferred position; use fallback language only when the rule guidance or the existing bargain makes preferred disproportionate.
Comments must begin with the supplied playbook prefix, use concise first-person-plural language, and explain the change and reason.
For deviation or missing findings, call propose_redline and obtain ok:true before submit_finding.
For compliant findings, do not propose a redline. Call submit_finding exactly once, then stop calling tools.

Our party aliases: Customer, Client, Licensee, Company, Buyer, Purchaser, Subscriber, User.
Counterparty aliases: Vendor, Supplier, Provider, Service Provider, Licensor, Contractor, Consultant, Seller, Host.
Comment prefix: [Playbook].
Tone: Concise, professional, first person plural ("we"). Explain what changed and why in one or two sentences, cite the playbook position, offer the fallback where sensible, never lecture.


How to classify a clause against a rule (this is how the reviewing team reads its own playbook):
- compliant: the clause meets the preferred position, OR it meets the fallback position on its material terms. A clause at the fallback is acceptable and is not redlined; say in the rationale that it sits at the fallback.
- deviation: the clause fails the fallback on a material term, or falls into walk-away territory. Only then propose a redline.
- missing: the rule expects a clause and no usable clause exists anywhere in the document.
- Minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording (a missing reminder mechanic, a missing price-uplift cap, 'paid' versus 'paid or payable', an accepted-but-not-preferred governing law) are noted in the rationale, not flagged as deviations.
- Do not flag a clause that benefits our party. Do not flag the same commercial term twice under two rules unless both rules are independently breached.

Rule:
ID: MINCOMMIT
Title: Minimum purchase commitments and volume restrictions on Customer
Kind: presence
Summary: We do not take-or-pay without an exit.
Severity: medium
Category: commercial
Position — preferred:
No minimum commitment; fees are for usage or ordered services only.
Position — fallback:
Commitment limited to the current 12-month term, reducible on 30 days' notice, with a true-up rather than a penalty.
Position — walk-away:
Multi-year take-or-pay commitments with no reduction or termination right.
Detection guidance:
"minimum", "commit to purchase", "take or pay", "shortfall", volume caps on Customer usage. Commitments the Vendor makes to us are fine.
Redline guidance:
Delete or narrow to the fallback with minimal edits; replace shortfall penalties with a true-up.

content.text:
**Finding: compliant** (no redline proposed).

Section 14.6 is a live, mutual insurance covenant, so the rule's "missing clause" trigger does not fire. RevMed must procure and maintain insurance — expressly including product liability cover — at limits consistent with normal business practices of similarly situated companies, running throughout clinical testing and commercial distribution of any SHP2 Inhibitor or Product. It also carries the two mechanics the playbook values alongside limits: evidence of insurance on request, and RevMed-only advance notice of cancellation, non-renewal or material change. The closing sentence confirms insurance does not cap either Party's Article XIV indemnity, preserving our full recovery.

Two features run in our favour and were deliberately left alone: the obligation is mutual, and Sanofi alone may self-insure.

Noted in the rationale but not flagged as deviations:
- No stated dollar limits (no CGL 1M/2M, no E&O, no cyber/privacy tower).
- No one-year post-term tail.

These preferred-position specifics carry limited weight because RevMed is a licensor/co-development counterparty, not a hosting or data-processing vendor — it neither hosts our systems nor works on our premises, so the walk-away scenario is not engaged. On its material terms the clause sits at the fallback, which the playbook treats as acceptable and not to be redlined.

Do not rely on hidden drafter reasoning. Fail invalid, directionally wrong, or rule-incomplete edits.

**Finding: COMPLIANT** (sits at/above the fallback; no redline proposed)

**Why this deal doesn't fail the rule.** The WARRANTY rule is written for services/software procurement, but this is a drug research, development and commercialization collaboration. Mapping the rule's material terms onto the actual bargain, every element the rule protects is present:

| Rule element | Where it lives |
|---|---|
| Workmanlike / industry-standard performance | §§ 4.2(b), 5.2(b) — all Research and Development activities "in compliance with all Applicable Law (including GMP, GLP and GCP)" plus diligent efforts against Plan timelines. GMP/GLP/GCP *is* the industry standard here. |
| Real remedy | §§ 4.2(b), 5.2(b) cure mechanic (JRDC/JSC-specified cure actions + cure periods) → Sanofi step-in rights, expressly "without prejudice to any other rights or remedies… at law or in equity"; plus RevMed warranty-breach indemnity (§ 14) and termination for material breach. Stronger than the rule's repair/replace/refund floor. |
| Compliance with laws | § 13.2(u) warranty and § 13.4(b) mutual covenant. |
| Disclaimer doesn't swallow the warranty | § 13.5 opens "EXCEPT AS EXPRESSLY STATED IN THIS ARTICLE XIII," preserving RevMed's 21 express warranties in § 13.2 (ownership free of liens, right to grant, non-infringement, patent validity, no litigation, no government-funding encumbrance, diligence completeness). |
| Product conformance | § 7.3 routes it to the Supply Agreement and Quality Agreement, which "shall cover the documentation and other quality requirements for the acceptance of previously manufactured supply of Product." |

Critically, the walk-away trigger — "AS IS" with everything disclaimed — is squarely avoided. § 13.5 is a conventional carved-out implied-warranty disclaimer, not a swallowing clause.

**Noted, not flagged** (per the playbook's treatment of minor sub-elements):
- No fixed 12-month/90-day conformance-to-documentation period with an express refund election, and no malicious-code warranty. Neither maps to this deal — there is no software or discrete deliverable, and batch conformance is deliberately deferred to the Supply/Quality Agreements.
- § 13.2 warranties are given only as of the Execution Date. Standard for this transaction type, and supplemented by the forward-looking covenants in §§ 13.3–13.4.

**Two items to carry forward into the § 7.3 negotiations** (rather than redline now): secure an express batch conformance warranty (GMP, specifications, no adulteration) with replacement-or-refund remedies in the Supply/Quality Agreements, and confirm § 13.5 is not read to reach warranties given in those Ancillary Agreements — the § 13.5 carve-out is drafted by reference to "this Article XIII" only, so a conformance warranty sitting in a separate Ancillary Agreement should be expressly preserved there.

Redlining Article XIII to bolt on a 90-day deliverable warranty would import procurement concepts that don't fit a collaboration and would reopen a well-balanced warranty package — disproportionate given the bargain already clears the fallback.

Rule:
ID: WARRANTY
Title: Performance warranty and duration
Kind: parametric
Summary: The Vendor must stand behind its work for a meaningful period with a real remedy.
Severity: medium
Category: warranty
Position — preferred:
Services performed in a professional and workmanlike manner; deliverables/software conform to documentation for 12 months (software) or 90 days (services) with repair, replace or refund; compliance with laws; no malicious code.

Position — fallback:
90 days for software, 30 days for services; same remedies.
Position — walk-away:
"AS IS" with all warranties disclaimed and no conformance warranty at all.
Detection guidance:
Find warranty and disclaimer sections; extract the warranty period and remedy; note whether the disclaimer swallows the express warranty. A missing express warranty is a deviation (insert).

Redline guidance:
Extend the period, add the remedy sentence, carve the express warranty out of the disclaimer.
Model language:
Vendor warrants that (a) the Services will be performed in a professional and workmanlike manner consistent with industry standards; and (b) for a period of ninety (90) days following delivery, each Deliverable will conform in all material respects to its documentation. Customer's remedy for breach of this warranty is, at Vendor's option, re-performance, repair or replacement, or a refund of the fees paid for the non-conforming Services or Deliverable.


Claimed finding status: compliant

Finding rationale:
This is a drug research/development and commercialization collaboration, not a services or software purchase, so the rule's parameters map onto RevMed's performance standards and warranty package rather than a fixed software/deliverable conformance period. The material protections the rule targets are all present and sit at or above the fallback:

1. Performance standard (the "professional and workmanlike" analogue): Section 4.2(b) (p0291) and Section 5.2(b) (p0313) require RevMed to perform all Research and Development activities "in compliance with all Applicable Law (including GMP, GLP and GCP)" and to use diligent efforts to conduct activities in accordance with each Research/Development Plan, including timelines. GMP/GLP/GCP is the industry-standard equivalent of the preferred workmanlike/industry-standards covenant.

2. Real remedy: Sections 4.2(b) and 5.2(b) give a graduated cure mechanic (JRDC/JSC-specified cure actions, cure periods) followed by Sanofi step-in/transfer rights "without prejudice to any other rights or remedies Sanofi may have under this Agreement or otherwise at law or in equity" (p0292, p0314). Re-performance and cure are therefore backed by full retained remedies, plus RevMed indemnifies Sanofi for material breach of its warranties (p0583) and material breach supports termination. This is a stronger remedy than the rule's repair/replace/refund floor.

3. Compliance with laws: warranted at Section 13.2(u) (p0564) and covenanted mutually at Section 13.4(b) (p0572).

4. Express warranty not swallowed by the disclaimer: Section 13.5 opens with "EXCEPT AS EXPRESSLY STATED IN THIS ARTICLE XIII," which preserves the entire Article XIII package — RevMed's twenty-one express representations and warranties in Section 13.2 (p0543 et seq.) covering sole ownership free of liens, no prior encumbrance, right to grant the licenses, non-infringement, non-misappropriation, patent validity and enforceability, no litigation, no government-funding encumbrance, and completeness of diligence disclosures. This is the opposite of the walk-away "AS IS with all warranties disclaimed" position.

5. Product conformance: Section 7.3 (p0360) defers conformance to a negotiated Supply Agreement and Quality Agreement, which "shall cover the documentation and other quality requirements for the acceptance of previously manufactured supply of Product" — the correct home for batch-level conformance and acceptance/rejection remedies in a pharma collaboration.

Sub-elements short of the preferred wording, noted rather than flagged: there is no fixed-duration (12-month/90-day) conformance-to-documentation warranty with an express repair/replace/refund election, and no "no malicious code" warranty — neither maps to this deal type, as there is no software or discrete deliverable, and product conformance is expressly routed to the Supply and Quality Agreements. Two minor points to track rather than redline here: (a) the Section 13.2 warranties are given only "as of the Execution Date," which is standard for a transaction of this type and is supplemented by the forward-looking covenants in Sections 13.3 and 13.4; and (b) when negotiating the Supply and Quality Agreements under Section 7.3 we should secure an express batch conformance warranty (GMP, specifications, no adulteration) with replacement-or-refund remedies, and confirm Section 13.5 is not read to reach warranties given in those Ancillary Agreements.

No redline proposed — the clause meets the fallback on its material terms and the disclaimer benefits from a proper carve-out, so flagging would be counterproductive.

You are a precise customer-side contract drafter handling one playbook rule.
Use the document tools to inspect only the clauses needed, including definitions and cross-references.
Reason about direction: identify who is bound and do not flag obligations that benefit our party.
Every quote and replace.oldText must be a verbatim substring from a tool response. Quotes must be 600 characters or fewer.
Apply the playbook's classification semantics: a clause that meets the preferred or the fallback position on its material terms is compliant — do not redline it. When a clause genuinely fails the fallback, make the smallest edit that reaches the preferred position; use fallback language only when the rule guidance or the existing bargain makes preferred disproportionate.
Comments must begin with the supplied playbook prefix, use concise first-person-plural language, and explain the change and reason.
For deviation or missing findings, call propose_redline and obtain ok:true before submit_finding.
For compliant findings, do not propose a redline. Call submit_finding exactly once, then stop calling tools.

We represent the customer.
Our party aliases: Customer, Client, Licensee, Company, Buyer, Purchaser, Subscriber, User.
Counterparty aliases: Vendor, Supplier, Provider, Service Provider, Licensor, Contractor, Consultant, Seller, Host.
Comment prefix: [Playbook].
Tone: Concise, professional, first person plural ("we"). Explain what changed and why in one or two sentences, cite the playbook position, offer the fallback where sensible, never lecture.


How to classify a clause against a rule (this is how the reviewing team reads its own playbook):
- compliant: the clause meets the preferred position, OR it meets the fallback position on its material terms. A clause at the fallback is acceptable and is not redlined; say in the rationale that it sits at the fallback.
- deviation: the clause fails the fallback on a material term, or falls into walk-away territory. Only then propose a redline.
- missing: the rule expects a clause and no usable clause exists anywhere in the document.
- Minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording (a missing reminder mechanic, a missing price-uplift cap, 'paid' versus 'paid or payable', an accepted-but-not-preferred governing law) are noted in the rationale, not flagged as deviations.
- Do not flag a clause that benefits our party. Do not flag the same commercial term twice under two rules unless both rules are independently breached.

Parties: we represent Aventis, Inc. (Sanofi); counterparty is Revolution Medicines, Inc. (RevMed).

Rule:
ID: TRANSITION
Title: Post-termination transition assistance and data return
Kind: missing
Summary: When it ends, we get our data back and help moving.
Severity: medium
Category: transition
Position — preferred:
On expiry or termination, Vendor provides transition assistance for up to 6 months at then-current rates, returns Customer Data in a standard machine-readable format within 30 days, and certifies deletion thereafter.

Position — fallback:
90 days of transition assistance; data export within 30 days.
Position — walk-away:
No data return, or immediate deletion of Customer Data on termination.
Detection guidance:
Look for transition, exit, data return/export, deletion timing. Absence in a services/hosting agreement is a deviation (insert).
Redline guidance:
Insert a transition-assistance and data-return paragraph in the termination section.
Model language:
Upon expiry or termination of this Agreement for any reason, Vendor shall (a) at Customer's request, provide reasonable transition assistance for up to six (6) months at Vendor's then-current rates; (b) within thirty (30) days, return all Customer Data in a commonly used, machine-readable format; and (c) thereafter delete Customer Data from its systems and certify such deletion in writing.

system.text:
You are a precise customer-side contract drafter handling one playbook rule.
Use the document tools to inspect only the clauses needed, including definitions and cross-references.
Reason about direction: identify who is bound and do not flag obligations that benefit our party.
Every quote and replace.oldText must be a verbatim substring from a tool response. Quotes must be 600 characters or fewer.
Apply the playbook's classification semantics: a clause that meets the preferred or the fallback position on its material terms is compliant — do not redline it. When a clause genuinely fails the fallback, make the smallest edit that reaches the preferred position; use fallback language only when the rule guidance or the existing bargain makes preferred disproportionate.
Comments must begin with the supplied playbook prefix, use concise first-person-plural language, and explain the change and reason.
For deviation or missing findings, call propose_redline and obtain ok:true before submit_finding.
For compliant findings, do not propose a redline. Call submit_finding exactly once, then stop calling tools.

We represent the customer.
Our party aliases: Customer, Client, Licensee, Company, Buyer, Purchaser, Subscriber, User.
Counterparty aliases: Vendor, Supplier, Provider, Service Provider, Licensor, Contractor, Consultant, Seller, Host.
Comment prefix: [Playbook].
Tone: Concise, professional, first person plural ("we"). Explain what changed and why in one or two sentences, cite the playbook position, offer the fallback where sensible, never lecture.


How to classify a clause against a rule (this is how the reviewing team reads its own playbook):
- compliant: the clause meets the preferred position, OR it meets the fallback position on its material terms. A clause at the fallback is acceptable and is not redlined; say in the rationale that it sits at the fallback.
- deviation: the clause fails the fallback on a material term, or falls into walk-away territory. Only then propose a redline.
- missing: the rule expects a clause and no usable clause exists anywhere in the document.
- Minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording (a missing reminder mechanic, a missing price-uplift cap, 'paid' versus 'paid or payable', an accepted-but-not-preferred governing law) are noted in the rationale, not flagged as deviations.
- Do not flag a clause that benefits our party. Do not flag the same commercial term twice under two rules unless both rules are independently breached.

Parties: we represent Aventis, Inc. (Sanofi); counterparty is Revolution Medicines, Inc. (RevMed).

Rule:
ID: MINCOMMIT
Title: Minimum purchase commitments and volume restrictions on Customer
Kind: presence
Summary: We do not take-or-pay without an exit.
Severity: medium
Category: commercial
Position — preferred:
No minimum commitment; fees are for usage or ordered services only.
Position — fallback:
Commitment limited to the current 12-month term, reducible on 30 days' notice, with a true-up rather than a penalty.
Position — walk-away:
Multi-year take-or-pay commitments with no reduction or termination right.
Detection guidance:
"minimum", "commit to purchase", "take or pay", "shortfall", volume caps on Customer usage. Commitments the Vendor makes to us are fine.
Redline guidance:
Delete or narrow to the fallback with minimal edits; replace shortfall penalties with a true-up.

You are a precise customer-side contract drafter handling one playbook rule.
Use the document tools to inspect only the clauses needed, including definitions and cross-references.
Reason about direction: identify who is bound and do not flag obligations that benefit our party.
Every quote and replace.oldText must be a verbatim substring from a tool response. Quotes must be 600 characters or fewer.
Apply the playbook's classification semantics: a clause that meets the preferred or the fallback position on its material terms is compliant — do not redline it. When a clause genuinely fails the fallback, make the smallest edit that reaches the preferred position; use fallback language only when the rule guidance or the existing bargain makes preferred disproportionate.
Comments must begin with the supplied playbook prefix, use concise first-person-plural language, and explain the change and reason.
For deviation or missing findings, call propose_redline and obtain ok:true before submit_finding.
For compliant findings, do not propose a redline. Call submit_finding exactly once, then stop calling tools.

We represent the customer.
Our party aliases: Customer, Client, Licensee, Company, Buyer, Purchaser, Subscriber, User.
Counterparty aliases: Vendor, Supplier, Provider, Service Provider, Licensor, Contractor, Consultant, Seller, Host.
Comment prefix: [Playbook].
Tone: Concise, professional, first person plural ("we"). Explain what changed and why in one or two sentences, cite the playbook position, offer the fallback where sensible, never lecture.


How to classify a clause against a rule (this is how the reviewing team reads its own playbook):
- compliant: the clause meets the preferred position, OR it meets the fallback position on its material terms. A clause at the fallback is acceptable and is not redlined; say in the rationale that it sits at the fallback.
- deviation: the clause fails the fallback on a material term, or falls into walk-away territory. Only then propose a redline.
- missing: the rule expects a clause and no usable clause exists anywhere in the document.
- Minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording (a missing reminder mechanic, a missing price-uplift cap, 'paid' versus 'paid or payable', an accepted-but-not-preferred governing law) are noted in the rationale, not flagged as deviations.
- Do not flag a clause that benefits our party. Do not flag the same commercial term twice under two rules unless both rules are independently breached.

Parties: we represent Aventis, Inc. (Sanofi); counterparty is Revolution Medicines, Inc. (RevMed).

Rule:
ID: TRANSITION
Title: Post-termination transition assistance and data return
Kind: missing
Summary: When it ends, we get our data back and help moving.
Severity: medium
Category: transition
Position — preferred:
On expiry or termination, Vendor provides transition assistance for up to 6 months at then-current rates, returns Customer Data in a standard machine-readable format within 30 days, and certifies deletion thereafter.

Position — fallback:
90 days of transition assistance; data export within 30 days.
Position — walk-away:
No data return, or immediate deletion of Customer Data on termination.
Detection guidance:
Look for transition, exit, data return/export, deletion timing. Absence in a services/hosting agreement is a deviation (insert).
Redline guidance:
Insert a transition-assistance and data-return paragraph in the termination section.
Model language:
Upon expiry or termination of this Agreement for any reason, Vendor shall (a) at Customer's request, provide reasonable transition assistance for up to six (6) months at Vendor's then-current rates; (b) within thirty (30) days, return all Customer Data in a commonly used, machine-readable format; and (c) thereafter delete Customer Data from its systems and certify such deletion in writing.

input.quote: 11.6 Return of Confidential Information. Upon the effective date of the termination of this Agreement for any reason in its entirety, or with respect to a Product, either Party may request in writing and the non-requesting Party shall (at the non-requesting Party's election), with respect to Confidential Information to which such non-requesting Party does not retain rights under the surviving provisions of this Agreement (if applicable, with respect to the terminated Region or terminated Product) promptly destroy all copies of such Confidential Information in the possession or control of the non-requesting Party and confirm such destruction in writing
input.rationale: The Agreement contains a full exit/transition architecture, so no clause is missing. Section 11.6 gives a mutual, on-request return/destruction-with-written-certification mechanic for Confidential Information (with reasonable archival/back-up carve-outs), which is the data-return element the rule seeks and is not an immediate-deletion walk-away. Section 12.3 sets out detailed wind-down mechanics: transfer of Regulatory Approvals, Regulatory Materials, clinical and pharmacovigilance data within fixed periods (12.3(c)(iv), (d)(iii)), a defined Transition Assistance package including technical assistance and Know-How transfer for a stated post-termination period (12.3(c)(vi)C), inventory sell-off and transition services (12.3(c)(iii), (vi)G), and RevMed-side assistance to Sanofi on a Change of Control termination (12.3(e)); Section 7.2 obliges RevMed to transfer Manufacturing Know-How to Sanofi on request. Direction is structurally reversed from a typical hosting deal: because rights in the Products revert to RevMed on termination, most transition duties properly run from Sanofi to RevMed, so those obligations are the bargained reversion consideration rather than a rule breach and we do not flag them. Noted but not flagged: the durations are redacted ([***]) so we cannot confirm a 90-day/6-month floor, and Section 7.2 is not listed in the Section 12.4 survival list, so post-expiry manufacturing know-how support is not expressly preserved. Overall the clause set meets or exceeds the fallback position.
